name: Trust
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Why Trust Is a Shortcut, Not a Weakness
lesson.summary: Introduces trust as a practical way people manage risk and act despite uncertainty, and explains why strangers rely on trusted intermediaries when they lack a shared history.
lesson.body:
Trust is what lets you act without being certain. When you hand your credit card to a waiter you cannot see, mail a letter and expect it to arrive, or believe a doctor's diagnosis without reviewing their medical training yourself, you are trusting: relying on someone or something to behave the way you expect, even though you cannot fully verify it in the moment and cannot force the outcome. Trust is not naivete. It is a practical tool for operating in a world where you cannot check everything yourself.

Think about what life would look like without it. Before every transaction you would need to personally verify the other party's honesty, competence, and intentions: audit the restaurant's kitchen, confirm the waiter's employment history, test the food for contamination. Almost nothing would get done. Trust is a shortcut that lets people cooperate and exchange value without paying the full cost of certainty. You accept some risk of being wrong in exchange for being able to act at all.

That tradeoff comes with a real cost: vulnerability. To trust someone is to give them an opportunity to disappoint you, whether through dishonesty, incompetence, or simple bad luck. This is why trust tends to come easier between people who expect to interact again. Game theorists have long noted that repeated relationships change behavior: if you know you will deal with the same supplier next month, cheating them today costs you future business, so there is a reason to behave well now. Trust with a stranger you will likely never see again is riskier precisely because that future consequence is missing.

Societies have built ways around the stranger problem without eliminating the need for trust itself. Instead, they concentrate it. Rather than trusting every individual merchant, you trust a credit card network to reverse a fraudulent charge. Rather than trusting a random buyer's promise to pay, a court system exists to enforce contracts. Rather than trusting a stranger's word about their identity, a government issues an ID card backed by its own authority. These trusted third parties, banks, courts, notaries, licensing boards, do not remove risk. They redirect it toward an institution that has reputation, legal accountability, or enforcement power an individual stranger lacks.

This arrangement works remarkably well in person, where reputation travels through communities, body language offers cues, and legal systems have clear jurisdiction. A shopkeeper who cheats regular customers loses business as word spreads locally; a stranger who cannot pay is noticed immediately because you are standing in front of them. These signals are so ordinary that it is easy to forget they are doing real work, quietly supplying the evidence that lets you extend trust without a formal guarantee.

The next chapter looks at what happens to trust when those in-person signals disappear and interactions move onto digital networks, where you often cannot see, hear, or locate the party on the other end at all.
